subject: mrcp-statistics
title: Study design, bias and confounding

steps.tx: A **confounder** is a factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome, which is not an intermediate step on the causal path. Confounding makes a crude association misleading. It can be handled by **randomisation**, restriction, matching, stratification or multivariable adjustment, but only for measured variables. Residual confounding persists when measurement is imperfect.

steps.tx: The diagram shows a **confounder** as a shared background factor at the top with arrows pointing to both **exposure** and outcome. Because it influences both sides, it creates an apparent distorted link between exposure and outcome shown by the dashed arrow. This **crude association** can mislead unless the confounder is handled by **randomisation** or adjustment for measured variables.
steps.say: This diagram explains confounding. A confounder is a background factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome, but it is not a step on the causal path between them. Because it touches both sides, it makes the crude link between exposure and outcome look stronger or weaker than it truly is. Good design handles confounders through randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification or adjustment, though residual confounding can persist when measurement is imperfect.

steps.tx: **Immortal time bias** occurs when follow-up time during which the outcome cannot occur is wrongly credited to the exposed group. Classifying people as exposed only after a later event, such as a first prescription, makes the drug look protective. The fix is a **time-dependent exposure** analysis, counting pre-exposure person-time as unexposed.

steps.tx: **Lead-time bias** arises when screening or testing diagnoses disease earlier, so survival measured from diagnosis looks longer even though the date of death is unchanged. **Length-time bias** is a separate problem, where screening preferentially detects slowly progressive cases. Mortality or incidence outcomes are the fairer test of screening.

steps.tx: **Regression to the mean** explains why an extreme first measurement, such as a single high blood pressure reading, tends to fall on repeat testing without treatment. **Berkson bias** is selection bias from hospital-based samples, where admission depends on both exposure and disease, producing spurious associations. Population-based controls reduce it.

steps.tx: **Non-differential misclassification** of exposure, where errors are equal across outcome groups, usually biases an association towards the null. Differential misclassification can push results in either direction. **Neyman bias** (prevalence-incidence bias) occurs when prevalent users are sampled, so early withdrawals are missed and mislabelled as unexposed.

Differential misclassification can push results in either direction. Neyman bias, also called prevalence-incidence bias, occurs when prevalent users are sampled, so early withdrawals are missed and mislabelled as unexposed.

vis.alt: Two panels of stacked bars. Truly, half of cases and half of controls were exposed, an odds ratio of 1. From memory, cases report four-fifths exposed and controls two-fifths, a false odds ratio of 6.
vis.caption: Recall bias is differential misclassification: unequal memory creates an association where none exists.
